docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Platforms for the exploitation of Earth Observation (EO) data have been developed by public and private companies in order to foster the usage of EO data and expand the market of Earth Observation-derived information. A fundamental principle of the platform operations concept is to move the EO data processing service’s user to the data and tools, as opposed to downloading, replicating, and exploiting data ‘at home’. In this scope, previous OGC activities initiated the development of an architecture to allow the ad-hoc deployment and execution of applications close to the physical location of the source data with the goal to minimize data transfer between data repositories and application processes.

The OGC published the Best Practice for Earth Observation Application Package (20-089r1), a document defining the Best Practice to package and deploy Earth Observation Applications in an Exploitation Platform. The document is targeting the implementation, packaging and deployment of EO Applications in support of collaborative work processes between developers and platform owners.

The Best Practice includes recommendations for the application design patterns, package encoding, container and data interfaces for data stage-in and stage-out strategies focusing on three main viewpoints: Application, Package and Platform.

The focus of this documentation set is on data interfaces for data stage-in and stage-out strategies.

docs.title: Earth Observation Applications
docs.text:
Earth Observation Applications typically offer functions that perform data operations like processing / reprocessing, projection, visualization or analysis. The applications can be written in a variety of coding languages (e.g. Python, R, Go, Java, C++, C#, shell scripts) and make use of specific software libraries (e.g. SNAP, GDAL, Orfeo Toolbox).

In the context of the Best Practice for Earth Observation Application Package, the application is treated as a black-box that according to its application design pattern must comply with data stage-in and data stage-out mechanisms defined.

docs.title: Staging Input and Output EO Products
docs.text:
EO product files come in different formats (e.g. GeoTIFF, HDF5, SAFE) and might have sub-items (e.g. metadata, bands, masks) that can be encoded in the same file or follow a given folder structure.

For example, SENTINEL-2 products are made available to users in the SENTINEL-SAFE format, including image data in JPEG2000 format, quality indicators (e.g. defective pixels mask), auxiliary data and metadata. The SAFE format wraps a folder containing image data in a binary data format and product metadata in XML. A SENTINEL-2 product refers to a directory folder that contains a collection of information that can include several files.

A main concern application developers face is the different approaches through which the products are made available (i.e. stage-in) to the applications. For example, applications might find the same exact folder structure and return the folder root or the main XML manifest file or have the folder structure compressed in a single archive file.

In general, the onus of navigating the input folder directory and programmatically reacting to how the file was staged-in by the platform is on application and the application developer needs to consider all possible cases when developing their read routines.

Conversely, the outputs of the application are fully managed by the developer that places the resulting files in an output directory. The only information the platform might receive about the output files is the file media type (formerly known as “MIME-type”) and is often missing critical information like spatial footprint, sub-items (e.g. masks, bands) and additional metadata (e.g. ground sample distance, orbit direction).

A good solution to represent the data manifest for input and output products is brought by the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC).

docs.title: SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC)
docs.text:
The STAC specification standardizes the way geospatial assets are exposed online and queried. A ‘spatiotemporal asset’ is any file that represents information about the earth captured in a certain space and time (e.g. satellites, planes, drones, balloons).

The STAC specification defines several objects:

  • STAC Catalog: STAC Catalog is a collection of STAC Items or other STAC Catalogs (sub-catalogs). The division of sub-catalogs is transparently managed by links to ease online browsing.
  • STAC Collection: extends the STAC Catalog with additional fields to describe a whole set of STAC Items that share properties and metadata. STAC Collections are meant to be compatible with OGC API — Features Collections (OGC 17-069r3).
  • STAC Item: a GeoJSON Feature with additional fields (e.g. time, geo), links to related entities and STAC Assets.
  • STAC Asset: is an object that contains a link to data associated with the STAC Item that can be downloaded or streamed (e.g. data, metadata, thumbnails) and can contain additional metadata. Similar to atom:link it has properties like href, title, description, type and roles; but, most significantly, it allows relative paths.

Most importantly the STAC specification can be implemented in a completely ‘static’ manner as flat local files located near the data enabling the application to access products assets (e.g. JPEG 2000 band file, auxiliary data, browse) with a relative path (something that was not possible using OpenSearch as defined by OGC 13-026r8, OGC 13-032r8).

The Best Practice for Earth Observation Application Package selected a STAC Catalog with STAC Item files as the data manifests format, for application that require staging input data and/or output results. Start with the quickstart, then follow the hands-on exercises. For implementation details, read the application manifest contract and CWL reference.

docs.title: Application data flow management
docs.text: The application consumes and produces STAC manifests in CWL Directory ports representing EO products. See OGC Best Practice 20-089r1, sections 7.3.1, 7.4 and 8.3 for the requirements and the platform flow for staging responsibilities.

docs.title: Stage-in
docs.text:
The application receives a directory containing catalog.json, linked STAC Items, and accessible asset files. It opens that catalog and resolves each asset href relative to its Item JSON, rather than the current working directory:

from pathlib import Path
import pystac
catalog = pystac.read_file(str(Path(staged_directory) / "catalog.json"))
item = next(catalog.get_items())  # This example processes one direct Item.
asset_path = item.assets["green"].get_absolute_href()

The application workflow's item input is a Directory. The wrapper exposes that input as a URI record, stages the referenced Item, and passes the resulting directory to the application. Internal workflow steps receive the staged directory through ordinary CWL connections; they do not each need an additional stage-in step. A directory used for scratch files is not automatically an EO product manifest.

docs.title: Stage-out
docs.text:
For each EO product output requiring staging, the application returns a directory with catalog.json, linked Items, and referenced result assets. Include geometry, bbox, and temporal metadata (datetime, or an interval with start_datetime and end_datetime) in each Item. The wrapper uploads the manifest and referenced assets and returns a URI record pointing to the uploaded catalog.

The training application returns stac_catalog: Directory; the staging tool returns s3_catalog_output: URI. Ordinary temporary directories are outside this product contract. Unreferenced files are not uploaded by the example stage-out implementation.

docs.title: Minimal output manifest
docs.text:
The following layout describes one result. The GeoTIFF must actually exist; JSON alone does not create it.

results/
├── catalog.json
└── scene/
    ├── scene.json
    └── otsu.tif

results/catalog.json:

{
  "stac_version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "Catalog",
  "id": "water-bodies",
  "description": "Water body detection results",
  "links": [
    {"rel": "root", "href": "./catalog.json", "type": "application/json"},
    {"rel": "item", "href": "./scene/scene.json", "type": "application/geo+json"}
  ]
}

results/scene/scene.json:

{
  "stac_version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "Feature",
  "id": "scene",
  "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[-119,38],[-118,38],[-118,39],[-119,39],[-119,38]]]},
  "bbox": [-119,38,-118,39],
  "properties": {"datetime": "2023-10-15T00:00:00Z"},
  "links": [
    {"rel": "root", "href": "../catalog.json", "type": "application/json"},
    {"rel": "parent", "href": "../catalog.json", "type": "application/json"}
  ],
  "assets": {
    "data": {
      "href": "./otsu.tif",
      "type": "image/tiff; application=geotiff; profile=cloud-optimized",
      "roles": ["data", "visual"]
    }
  }
}

Here ./otsu.tif resolves to results/scene/otsu.tif. Replace the illustrative footprint and acquisition time with metadata for your actual output. Only declare the COG media type for a cloud optimized GeoTIFF.

docs.title: Validate before staging
docs.text:
From the repository root, set catalog_path to the generated catalog:

hatch run python - <<'PYCODE'
from pathlib import Path
import pystac
catalog_path = "notebooks/staged/catalog.json"
catalog = pystac.read_file(catalog_path)
catalog.validate_all()
for item in catalog.get_items(recursive=True):
    for asset in item.assets.values():
        href = asset.get_absolute_href()
        assert href is not None
        if href.startswith("file://"):
            from urllib.parse import unquote, urlparse
            href = unquote(urlparse(href).path)
        if "://" not in href:
            assert Path(href).is_file(), href
print("STAC metadata and local asset paths validated")
PYCODE

Schema validation may fetch schemas over the network. It checks metadata, while the path checks verify local assets; neither checks pixel values or remote asset accessibility. See example limitations and troubleshooting.

docs.title: CWL interfaces and execution
docs.text: The examples use CWL 1.2. The processing interface uses local Directory objects; wrapping changes the EO input to a URI record and adds staging parameters. A URI record's value is converted to a command argument or environment variable by the CWL bindings.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Port Application Wrapped workflow / staging Meaning item Directory URI record Local catalog folder, or remote STAC Item URL to stage aoi OGC BBox record Same Four values in west, south, east, north order; crs: CRS84 (longitude, latitude) epsg Enum, default "4326" Same CRS of AOI coordinates; only "4326" is accepted here bands Array of band enums Same Use exactly two ordered bands: green, then nir08 for the Landsat example stac_catalog Output Directory Input to stage-out Folder containing the output catalog and assets reference — Stage-in URI record URL of one STAC Item, not a search response or Catalog endpoint_url — URI record S3 API endpoint reachable from the stage-out container s3_bucket, sub_path — Strings Existing bucket and destination prefix aws_access_key_id, aws_secret_access_key, region_name — Strings Storage credentials and region another_input — String, templates only Demonstration parameter; use training; not used to process data s3_catalog_output — Stage-out output URI record Uploaded root catalog location

Application job shape:

item:
  class: Directory
  path: /absolute/path/to/staged
aoi:
  class: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eoap/schemas/main/ogc.yaml#BBox
  bbox: [-118.985, 38.432, -118.183, 38.938]
  crs: CRS84
epsg: "4326"
bands: [green, nir08]

Use the complete tracked processing input example and wrapped input example. Their URI records have the following shape:

reference:
  class: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eoap/schemas/main/string_format.yaml#URI
  value: https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1/collections/landsat-c2-l2/items/LC09_L2SP_042033_20231015_02_T1

URI records and module-defined band/EPSG enums are embedded in the CWL. The shared OGC BBox schema is still imported from eoap/schemas/main/ogc.yaml, so loading the document can require network access. Pin or vendor that schema if your deployment needs an immutable offline dependency.

docs.title: Run the tools
docs.text:
Run these commands from notebooks/, after configuring the environment in Quickstart. The CLI staging files are used by notebook 04; templates/ contains the demonstration tools used by notebook 05, including a separate single-file downloader.

Create stage-in-params.yaml using the reference record above, then run:

hatch run cwltool --podman --outdir staged-run cwl-cli/stage-in.cwl stage-in-params.yaml

Read the emitted CWL JSON's staged.location. Copy cwl-workflow/typed-inputs.yaml to processing-params.yaml and set item.path to that directory's absolute path. Relative CWL paths resolve against the job file; the example's ../staged assumes notebook 03 has created that folder.

hatch run cwltool --podman --outdir processing-run \
  'cwl-workflow/app-water-bodies.cwl#water-bodies-detection' processing-params.yaml

Use the emitted stac_catalog.location for stage-out's stac_catalog.path. Create stage-out-params.yaml:

stac_catalog:
  class: Directory
  path: /absolute/path/from/stac_catalog/location
s3_bucket: results
sub_path: run-004-001
aws_access_key_id: training
aws_secret_access_key: training-secret
region_name: us-east-1
endpoint_url:
  class: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eoap/schemas/main/string_format.yaml#URI
  value: http://host.containers.internal:9000

hatch run cwltool --podman --outdir stage-out-run cwl-cli/stage-out.cwl stage-out-params.yaml

For end-to-end execution, run notebook 05 to generate .main.cwl, copy cwl-workflow/wrapped-inputs.yaml to wrapped-params.yaml, and update its storage configuration using Quickstart:

hatch run cwltool --validate .main.cwl
hatch run cwltool --podman --outdir wrapped-run .main.cwl wrapped-params.yaml

Notebook 05 uses eoap-cwlwrap==0.32.0's Python wrap API and cwl-loader==0.27.0 serialization; no cwltool --pack is needed. Its generated input/output tables are the authority for the composed workflow's port names. The wrapper's command-line plugin separately requires transpiler-mate-runtime.

docs.title: Example limitations
docs.text:
These are training examples, not a general batch processor:

  • Processing takes the first direct Item in the input Catalog. Supply exactly one Item; additional Items are not processed.
  • Stage-out uses get_items() without recursive traversal. Use direct Items with local relative asset paths; nested catalogs and remotely hosted output assets are not handled by this uploader.
  • Input assets need a data role and EO band metadata with the requested common_name. Landsat uses nir08; the Sentinel-2 notebook uses nir.
  • Band order controls (first - second) / (first + second). Use green followed by NIR. The enum allows green, nir, nir08, but the array schema does not enforce exactly two entries.
  • The AOI must overlap the selected scene and contain finite pixels for Otsu thresholding. The CWL binding requires a four-coordinate BBox; this example supports CRS84/4326 AOIs.
  • The output is a uint8 water mask (1 above the Otsu threshold, 0 otherwise), with the input acquisition time and a footprint derived from the output raster. It does not implement cloud masking or a scientific accuracy assessment.
  • Stage-out uploads referenced assets only. Reusing a destination prefix can overwrite matching objects; use a fresh prefix. Uploads are not transactional, and failures can leave partial results.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: The Best Practice for Earth Observation Application Package addresses data flow management of the input and output EO Products files by defining rules for the data stage-in and data stage-out for Applications that require staged files and/or generate files that need to be staged-out.

docs.title: Data stage-in definition
docs.text: Data stage-in is the process to retrieve the inputs and make these available for the processing. Processing inputs are provided as catalogue references and the Platform is responsible for translating those references into inputs available as files for the local processing.

docs.title: Data stage-out definition
docs.text: Data stage-out is the process to upload the output files generated by the processing onto external system(s), and make them available for later usage. The Platform retrieves the processing outputs and automatically stores them onto an external persistent storage. Additionally, the Platform should publish the metadata of the outputs onto a Catalogue and provide their references as an output.

docs.title: Application Data Flow Management
docs.text:
The Application data flow management relies on the rules:

  • The computational workflow data interfaces use the Spatio Temporal Asset Catalog (STAC) to describe the EO data inputs and generated results

  • Stage-in

    • All input parameters of the CWL CommandLineTool that require the staging of EO products shall be of type Directory.
    • All input parameters of the CWL Workflow that require the staging of EO products shall be of type Directory.
    • Applications find a STAC catalog.json file

  • Stage-out

    • Applications produce a STAC catalog.json in output directories representing EO products to be staged out
    • The outputs field of the Workflow that requires the stage-out of the generated products shall be of type Directory.

docs.title: Platform Data Flow Management
docs.text:
A Platform is responsible for the data flow management by using a local catalogue encoded using the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) specification as a data manifest for application inputs and outputs.

The local catalogue provides knowledge about the input and output files data contents like spatial footprint, sub-items (e.g. masks, bands) and additional metadata.

docs.title: Wrapping the Application Package
docs.text:
Wrap an Application Package:

  • plug a stage-in step for application workflow inputs representing staged EO products (Directory in this example)
  • plug a stage-out step for application workflow outputs representing EO products to persist (Directory in this example)

The outcome is a wrapped CWL workflow that takes:

  • the application package parameters
  • any stage-in/stage-out parameters the platform may need to perform these operations

Wrapping changes the external EO input to a URI record while retaining the application's internal Directory interface. Internal steps consume those directories through CWL connections. See the application contract and typed CWL interfaces.

docs.text: The platform translates an EO product reference into the application's local STAC manifest, then persists the results. See OGC Best Practice 20-089r1, section 9.4.

docs.title: Stage-in
docs.text:
The example downloads a referenced STAC Item and its assets, rewrites local paths, and saves a self contained catalog. The general platform model can also support remotely accessible assets; the training tool downloads them.

PlantUML source

docs.title: Stage-out
docs.text:
The application creates a local catalog describing its output. The example uploads referenced assets and Item JSON, rewrites their locations to S3, and uploads the root catalog last. It does not register results in a separate searchable catalog service or implement an OGC API Processes endpoint.

PlantUML source

docs.title: Water body detection example
docs.text:
This diagram matches app-water-bodies.cwl: the application workflow has one node_detect step. Cropping, NDWI calculation, Otsu thresholding, and STAC creation happen inside that step. There is no CWL scatter in this implementation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Use a Linux workstation with Python 3.11 or 3.12, Git, Hatch, Podman, and Graphviz (dot). The notebooks use Python syntax requiring at least 3.9; use the versions above for this training environment. Install Hatch with python3 -m pip install --user hatch, and install Podman and Graphviz through your operating system package manager.

Podman must be able to run containers as your user. Check podman info and dot -V. Internet access is required for Python packages, container images, the shared OGC schema, and public STAC assets. Stage-in downloads all assets for the selected scene, so allow several GB of free disk space; download time depends on the scene and connection.

docs.title: Create the notebook environment
docs.text:
From the repository root:

hatch env create
hatch run python -m ipykernel install --user --name stac-eoap --display-name "STAC EOAP"
hatch run jupyter lab notebooks

Select the STAC EOAP kernel. Run notebooks 01–05 in order, with their working directory set to notebooks/. Check os.getcwd() in the kernel before executing. Notebooks 01 and 02 create catalogs in that directory; notebook 03 creates staged/; notebook 04 writes CWL job files and runs/; notebook 05 generates .main.cwl.

If your environment restricts writes to your home directory, set HATCH_ENV_TYPE_VIRTUAL_PATH to a writable directory before creating the environment. Use a Jupyter installation whose kernels are writable as well.

The Hatch environment installs training dependencies without installing this repository as a Python package; it contains documentation and notebooks rather than an importable stac_eoap module.

docs.title: Provide S3 storage
docs.text:
Notebooks 03–04 and the wrapped workflow require a pre-existing writable bucket. Their original SeaweedFS endpoint is a deployment-specific example, not a service included in this repository. You can use an existing S3 service or the local MinIO setup below.

Start a local training instance with persistent storage:

podman volume create stac-eoap-s3
podman run -d --name stac-eoap-s3 \
  -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001 \
  -e MINIO_ROOT_USER=training \
  -e MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD=training-secret \
  -v stac-eoap-s3:/data \
  quay.io/minio/minio:RELEASE.2025-04-22T22-12-26Z \
  server /data --console-address ":9001"

Open http://localhost:9001, sign in with the training credentials above, and create the results bucket. The S3 API listens on port 9000, while port 9001 serves the console. See the MinIO container documentation.

Use these values in the S3 configuration cells in notebooks 03 and 04, and in a private copy of wrapped-inputs.yaml:

Parameter Value s3_bucket results sub_path A new prefix per run, such as run-005-001 aws_access_key_id training aws_secret_access_key training-secret region_name us-east-1 endpoint_url.value, notebook 03 on the host http://localhost:9000 endpoint_url.value, notebook 04 and wrapped CWL containers http://host.containers.internal:9000

Podman normally supplies host.containers.internal to reach the host. Verify this from a container before running stage-out; for remote Podman or another container engine, provide an address reachable from the actual execution host. localhost inside a processing container refers to that container.

These credentials are for local training. For another service, replace the endpoint, region and credentials and ensure permission to upload objects and read results. Keep real credentials out of committed input files and saved notebook outputs. This tool passes explicit credentials and does not expose a session-token input.

docs.title: Run and inspect
docs.text:
Follow the hands-on sequence, or use the CWL commands. A successful application run produces a local catalog and otsu.tif; stage-out returns a record such as {"value": "s3://results/run-005-001/catalog.json"}.

Use the S3 console to inspect that prefix: it should contain catalog.json, an Item JSON, and the referenced GeoTIFF. An s3:// URI is an authenticated object-storage reference, not a browser download URL. See validation for metadata and asset checks and troubleshooting for recovery.

To stop local storage, run podman stop stac-eoap-s3; resume it with podman start stac-eoap-s3. The named volume retains uploaded data.

docs.title: Troubleshooting and recovery
docs.text: Symptom Check and recovery Imports fail or the wrong Python runs Select the STAC EOAP kernel; check sys.executable. Recreate the Hatch environment after dependency changes. Relative files or templates are missing Check os.getcwd() is notebooks/. Resolve job file paths against the job file's directory. Podman cannot start a CWL container Run podman info, check image pull access and available disk space. The examples explicitly select Podman; using Docker requires changing that runtime setting. Graphviz plots fail Install the system dot executable; the Python graphviz package alone is insufficient. Static SVG documentation does not need Graphviz. STAC read/download gets HTTP 403 or times out Check the Item URL, provider access/signing requirements, and network connectivity from the execution environment. Stage-in uses 60-second HTTP timeouts and up to three download attempts; this is not an overall job deadline. Missing band or an asset-related AttributeError Inspect asset roles and EO common_name metadata. Use green,nir08 for the Landsat scene. The current example can dereference a missing asset before reporting its intended missing-band error. Crop does not overlap or Otsu has no finite pixels Check AOI west/south/east/north order, CRS84 coordinates, scene footprint, and valid raster pixels. Use the provided scene and AOI together first. S3 connection fails Use the API port, not the console port. Check endpoint reachability from the host for notebook 03 and from the CWL container for notebook 04 and wrapping. Container localhost does not reach the host. S3 reports missing bucket or access denied Create the bucket first; check credentials, region and upload/read permissions. These examples require explicit key/secret inputs and do not support session tokens. Results exist but the catalog cannot be opened Inspect the root catalog's Item links and each asset href; use an S3-aware client with the same endpoint and credentials. A custom endpoint is not encoded in an s3:// URI.

docs.title: Logs and safe reruns
docs.text:
Capture a CLI run's output and errors separately:

hatch run cwltool --podman --outdir wrapped-run .main.cwl wrapped-params.yaml > result.json 2> run.log

Run from notebooks/. Add --debug when investigating a failure, and inspect the failed step's command and traceback in run.log. Review logs and notebook outputs for credentials before sharing them.

After an interrupted notebook, restart the kernel, confirm its working directory, and rerun prerequisite cells. Move an incomplete generated output directory aside before rerunning; notebooks 01–02 write into the working directory, and notebook 03 reuses staged/. Keep previous successful results separate. If a stage-out rerun reports /tmp/catalog already exists, a previous failure left the tool's temporary copy behind; in notebook 03's host process, move that temporary directory aside after checking it belongs to this run. A fresh CWL container has its own temporary directory.

Use a new CWL --outdir and S3 sub_path for each retry. Stage-out uploads assets and Items before the root catalog, so an interrupted upload can leave objects without a complete manifest. Inspect the old prefix, then remove only that failed run's objects if desired. Verify metadata and referenced assets using validation before treating a returned URI as a complete result.

docs.title: Validation and documentation maintenance
docs.text: Run commands from the repository root unless stated otherwise. These commands let you generate evidence for your own checkout; historical run paths from another machine are not an acceptance test.

docs.title: Documentation and CWL
docs.text:
hatch run mkdocs build --strict
hatch run cwl-docs --validate --output /tmp/stac-cwl-docs

The module-local generator checks metadata, descriptions, embedded module types and the approved shared OGC import, validates each tracked CWL document, and renders port/type reference Markdown. It does not prove that an application run or storage upload succeeds. It is not a claim of compatibility with transpiler-mate's cwl2markdown. Its rendered files are review artifacts outside the site; CWL interfaces provides the site reference.

docs.title: Notebook execution
docs.text:
Configure S3 in notebooks 03–04 first. From notebooks/, execute each notebook in order and keep executed copies outside the source directory:

mkdir -p ../artifacts/notebooks
hatch run jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute \
  --ExecutePreprocessor.kernel_name=stac-eoap \
  --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=3600 \
  --output-dir=../artifacts/notebooks \
  '01 EO Products as Input Data.ipynb'

Repeat for notebooks 02, 03, 04 and 05. Review each exit status and the executed outputs. These runs fetch remote data, use disk space, and upload results for notebooks 03–04. Notebook 05 generates the composed workflow; then use the wrapped execution command with a fresh S3 prefix. Store its result.json and run.log alongside the executed notebooks, after reviewing them for credentials.

For application acceptance, validate the local catalog with the STAC validation snippet, inspect the raster, and verify that uploaded Catalog/Item links and assets are readable with your configured endpoint. CWL schema validation alone does not verify these properties.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
The checked-in SVGs are generated from the adjacent .puml sources in docs/assets/diagrams/. Pages embed SVGs directly; readers and MkDocs do not need PlantUML or a Mermaid plugin.

Install Java and obtain a PlantUML jar. From the repository root:

java -jar /path/to/plantuml.jar -tsvg docs/assets/diagrams/*.puml

These sequence diagrams render without Graphviz. Commit both source and generated SVG after an edit, inspect the rendered diagrams, and run the strict site build. See PlantUML command-line usage.
